message.reasoning:
I am reviewing the Monopoly game state to determine the best action.

I am p2 with $245 and only one opponent left. I own two hotels on dark blues and three reds with two houses each. Most of my other properties are mortgaged. The opponent has $1003 and two hotels on reds.

The opponent has a full green monopoly and several other properties. They do not own the pink monopoly.

The opponent owns the brown monopoly with hotels on Mediterranean and Baltic. The green monopoly is unmortgaged with zero houses.

The plan is to target the opponent's Boardwalk hotel for a kill shot if their liquidation is low enough. Trading for Pennsylvania Avenue, States Avenue, or Vermont and Connecticut should be avoided. Building or unmortgaging must not reduce cash below the $450 Baltic hotel rent cushion.

The opponent's liquidation value is roughly $2,233. That includes $1,003 cash plus buildings and deeds. This figure will determine whether the Boardwalk hotel can be captured for a kill shot.

The opponent survives the Boardwalk hotel by $233. The Pennsylvania Avenue hotel is only $1,500 and would not kill them. I am on ILLINOIS_AVENUE while they are on NEW_YORK_AVENUE. My cash is $245. I will not build, unmortgage, or trade this turn.

I am on Illinois Avenue. I need to roll 17 or more spaces to pass GO and collect $200 before landing on Baltic Avenue.

I am correcting the board distance. From Illinois Avenue, the maximum roll of 12 spaces lands on Chance at space 36. Passing GO is impossible from this position.

The maximum roll of 12 spaces from Illinois Avenue lands on Park Place, my own property. I will end this turn and roll again next turn. I cannot reach Baltic Avenue from here. The spaces between here and Baltic include Water Works, Marvin Gardens, Pacific, and North Carolina, all owned by the opponent.

The opponent owns both utilities. Rent on Water Works would be ten times the dice roll if I land there. The three unmortgaged greens are all unimproved, so their rent is doubled: Marvin Gardens $44, Pacific $52, and North Carolina $52.

The next roll from Illinois Avenue is safe. Even a $40 Water Works rent is manageable with $245 cash. The real danger is the Baltic hotel at $450 later. I will not build more reds this turn. The goal is to drain the opponent so the Boardwalk hotel can kill them.

The opponent is on New York Avenue. From there they can land on my red properties with two houses, but they cannot reach my dark blues this turn. I am calculating the rent for those reds.

Standard Monopoly rent for two houses on the reds is $250 on Kentucky and Indiana, and $300 on Illinois. That matches the earlier estimates. A single hit on one of those properties would drain enough cash to kill the opponent with the Boardwalk hotel. Building three houses would raise rent to $700 or $750, which would definitely kill them but costs $150 per house. The current build is even at two houses each.

Building one house on a single red property is legal under the even-building rule. The cost is $150, leaving $95 cash. If the opponent lands there, they would pay $700 to $750 in rent. That would drop their liquidation value below the Boardwalk hotel price of $2,000 and guarantee a kill.

The upgrade is unnecessary. Two houses on the reds already exceed the $234 drain threshold, so a single hit would still kill the opponent. Building one house would cost $150 and leave only $95 cash. Selling that house later would recover only $75, creating a net loss of $75. That money is needed for the Baltic Avenue rent cushion.

The revised plan is to wait until after passing GO, when cash reaches $445. If the opponent lands on a red property before then, I will sell one house on Illinois for $75 and keep the other two reds at two houses each. This avoids building now and prevents uneven destruction of the red drain. Unmortgaging the mortgaged properties would cost too much with only $245 in cash.

I am calculating the exact unmortgage costs for each property. New York Avenue, B&O Railroad, Ventnor Avenue, Pennsylvania Avenue, and Short Line all require $110 to $176 to unmortgage. Unmortgaging any of these would burn cash that I need for the Baltic rent cushion. I also notice that I own the entire pink and orange monopolies, but they are all mortgaged.

Unmortgaging all three orange properties would cost $308, which exceeds my $245 cash. I cannot build on mortgaged properties anyway.

I am considering trading with the opponent. They have a full green monopoly but no houses. They could build greens if they had cash, yet they have not done so. Perhaps the game only allows building on your own turn, and they have been ending turns instead.

Green houses would be devastating. Three houses on Marvin Gardens would rent $850, and three on Pacific or North Carolina would rent $900 each. The opponent has roughly an 8-in-36 chance of landing on a red property next turn. If they miss, they could build greens and kill me quickly. I am considering trading to acquire their green properties or otherwise prevent them from developing that monopoly.

I am weighing specific trades to acquire the opponent's green monopoly. They already hold Oriental and Virginia, so I could offer States Avenue for their pink monopoly. I could also offer Vermont and Connecticut for their light blue monopoly. The goal is to prevent them from building greens and killing me.

Trading away my dark blue hotels or red properties would be suicide. The opponent already has $1,003 to build greens, so any trade must offer far more than an undeveloped green monopoly plus cash. They will likely reject a deal that breaks their green monopoly for mortgaged junk. I am also considering whether proposing a trade consumes my action and leaves me with another decision if the offer is rejected.

Rejected trades consume the action but leave another decision available. A bad offer wastes a turn, and deception is futile against a single opponent who can see the board.

The opponent could build one house on each green property for $600, leaving them with roughly $403. That would raise green rent to about $120–$130, which I might survive.

The opponent can only build one house on each green property, leaving them with roughly $403. Two houses on two greens would leave them with only $3 cash. I cannot stop them from building, so I must bankrupt them first. I am confirming that this is my post-turn phase.

I am on Illinois Avenue and have already rolled. I will end this turn.

Selling the house on Illinois Avenue would drop rent to $100. That is too low to kill the opponent with the Boardwalk hotel, which needs roughly $2,133 after rent. The opponent has a 4-in-36 chance of landing there, making it the most likely red hit. I will keep the house and avoid building now.

I need to choose a legal Monopoly action.

I have $245 and a dark blue hotel monopoly. The opponent has $1003 and light blue hotels. I am bankrupting the last opponent.

I am calculating the opponent's liquidation value to confirm the kill shot. The Boardwalk hotel is worth $2000. I need to verify whether the opponent's cash is still $1003.

I am tallying the opponent's properties. I estimate selling a light blue hotel returns about $125.

I am now calculating the opponent's mortgage values. Mediterranean and Baltic are each worth $30. Reading Railroad is worth $100. Oriental is worth $50. Electric Company is worth $75.

Virginia is worth $80. Penn RR is worth $100. Water Works is worth $75. Marvin Gardens is worth $140. Pacific and North Carolina are each worth $150.

The total mortgage value of all unmortgaged properties is $980.

The opponent's total liquidation is $2233. The Boardwalk hotel rent is $2000, so a $234 drain would bankrupt them. The Park Place hotel rent is only $1500, which is not enough to kill. I am now checking the red color group rent values with two houses.

Red property rent with two houses is confirmed at $250, $250, and $300. The opponent is on New York Avenue. I am mapping the board to identify which spaces they will land on next.

The opponent can land on my red properties on rolls of 3, 5, or 6. They will hit Kentucky for $250, Indiana for $250, and Illinois for $300.

The opponent has a one-in-three chance of landing on my red properties. A $250 or $300 hit would drop their liquidation below the $2000 Boardwalk threshold and guarantee a bankruptcy. They cannot reach my dark blue hotels this turn because the maximum roll is only twelve spaces. I am now deciding what legal action to take.

I cannot trade property with buildings again. Building houses is too expensive with only $245 cash. Unmortgaging would waste money. Trading Pennsylvania Avenue would complete their greens. Trading States Avenue would complete their pinks. Trading Vermont or Connecticut would complete their light blue monopoly, which they already own.

I cannot trade property with buildings again. Building a house costs $150, and I only have $245 cash. I am checking whether the even-building rule allows adding one house at a time or requires building all three red properties to the same level first.

Building one house on a red property would cost $150 and leave only $95 cash. The rent would jump from $250 or $300 to $700 or $750. That would bankrupt the opponent if they land on a three-house red, but they might not land there. I am also weighing the risk of owing rent on the opponent's Baltic hotel.

The opponent has no color-group monopolies. They lack a pink or light-blue set, so their only high rents are the Baltic hotel at $450 and the Mediterranean hotel at $250. I am on Illinois.

I am now planning my next roll from Illinois. I will pass Water Works and Marvin Gardens, which would cost only $40 and $24. I will also pass Pacific and North Carolina. The only spaces I might land on are Ventnor, which is mortgaged and not mine, and Go to Jail.

I will not land on the opponent's Baltic hotel or Mediterranean hotel next turn. The maximum roll from Illinois is twelve spaces, which only reaches Chance. I will also not land on my own hotels in a way that matters. Building one house would leave me with $95 cash for one turn, but a bad Community Chest or Chance card could still bankrupt me.

A three-house red rent would still leave the opponent with enough cash to pay. Even a hotel on a red property would not bankrupt them. Red properties cannot directly kill the opponent; they only drain cash and force asset sales that make the Boardwalk hotel kill possible.

Current two-house red rents already drop the opponent's liquidation below $2000, so a subsequent Boardwalk hit would bankrupt them. Building more houses is unnecessary and wastes money. The only possible benefit is forcing the opponent to sell more assets and become vulnerable to the Park Place hotel.

Three houses on Illinois at $750 would bankrupt the opponent even against the Park Place hotel. Three houses on Kentucky and Indiana at $700 leaves them only $33 short of the Park Place threshold, so they survive that kill but still lose to Boardwalk.

Building one house on Illinois would cost $150 and leave $95 cash. This would make the opponent bankruptable by both the Park Place and Boardwalk hotels after a red hit, rather than only by Boardwalk. The probability of landing on Illinois from New York Avenue is about 14 percent.

The probability of landing on any red property is 33 percent. Building one house on Illinois would raise the rent from $300 to $750, but that only matters if the opponent lands on Park Place before Boardwalk or if Boardwalk is unavailable. Both hotels are currently occupied, so neither can be reached this turn. Leaving only $95 cash is risky because a bad card or landing could bankrupt me.

I need nineteen spaces to reach Baltic from Illinois, so I cannot land there this turn. I am also considering a Chance card that might send me to Boardwalk or Jail. My current cash of $245 is still too low to pay the $450 rent on Baltic.

The prior plan was to pass Go and sell one house on Illinois before landing on Baltic. That would yield $445, which is five dollars short of the $450 rent. Building another house now would leave only $95 cash. After passing Go, that would total $295, still short of $450. Selling three houses at half price would raise the balance to $520, covering the rent and leaving a seventy-dollar surplus.

Selling one house on Illinois would leave the red properties at one, two, and two houses. The rent would drop to one hundred dollars on Illinois and two hundred fifty dollars on Kentucky and Indiana. That still drains the opponent's liquidation below two thousand dollars, so the Boardwalk hotel kill remains viable without building.

I will not build or unmortgage. I am now considering trading mortgaged properties to acquire the opponent's hotels on Mediterranean and Baltic, which would remove the main bankruptcy threat.

The opponent will not trade their hotels, and they will not give cash. Any trade that would remove the threat of their Mediterranean or Baltic hotels would require offering something too valuable in return. Acquiring St Charles or other properties would be useless.

I am now weighing which mortgaged properties to offer in exchange for cash. The opponent already owns both utilities and two railroads, so those would not help them. The only potentially useful mortgaged set is the orange group, which they do not yet own.

No trade is viable. The opponent would only accept offers that help them more than me, and giving them an orange or yellow monopoly would arm them against me. The previous illegal trade note means I should simply end my turn. Selling one house on Illinois for seventy-five dollars would raise cash to three hundred twenty dollars.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.
